corpus_gaps: The Evidence Ordinance is not in the corpus, so the 'when required to do so by law' limb of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) cannot be mapped to a concrete disclosure-compelling or privilege provision; only the internal cross-reference in s.31 rule (36)(b) (inspection of a notary's records by named officers) and s.21(3) (production of documents at a misconduct inquiry) sit inside the corpus.

No provision in the corpus governs who may inspect, or obtain a copy of, a will held in a notary's protocol during the testator's lifetime; the Wills Ordinance No. 21 of 1844 as held in the corpus (7 sections) has nothing on custody, revocability or the ambulatory character of a will.

The Notaries Ordinance does not define 'employer' (s.43 defines only 'Council of Legal Education', 'High Court Judge' and 'Registrar-General'), so identifying the testator as the notary's employer rests on the ordinary meaning of the word plus the facts, not on a definition section.
Professional-conduct rules for attorneys-at-law and notaries made outside the Notaries Ordinance are not in the corpus.

The text of Notaries Ordinance s.34 as it stood in October 2018 is not in the corpus. 31-2022 s.17 repealed and substituted the whole section, and the only other fines instrument held for this Ordinance, the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005, carries just the Schedule-driven amending formula in its s.2, so no penalty wording for breach of the section 31 rules can be sourced for the matter date.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
provisions.why_relevant: This is the notarial secrecy rule and it decides the question. Whether a named person executed a will before the notary, and the date and number of that will, is knowledge the notary came by in the execution of his office. Rule (1) forbids him to divulge it and admits only two exits: the express permission of his employer, or a legal compulsion to disclose. Neither is present where the testator is alive, has given no permission, and no court order or statutory demand has been made.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 has been amended many times (20-1976 s.10, 47-2011 ss.2-3, 31-2022 s.16, 6-2024 s.3), but none of those amending sections touches rule (1). Rule (1) stands as enacted in 1907 and was in force at 2018-10.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed or instrument executed or acknowledged before him, to which shall be attached his signature and those of the party and witnesses to the original deed or instrument, and he shall keep a register thereof with a convenient index for the purpose of easy reference; and every such register shall be substantially in the form F in the Second Schedule, but in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the instrument shall be inserted in the register.
provisions.why_relevant: Supports the characterisation of the notary's knowledge as official rather than personal: he holds the will as protocol because his office obliges him to. It also shows that the Ordinance itself withholds the particulars of wills, recording only their number and date in the register kept for inspection, which is consistent with reading rule (1) strictly against disclosure of a will. It is not needed to reach the conclusion.
provisions.temporal_note: Rule (24) is unamended by 20-1976, 47-2011, 31-2022 or 6-2024 and was in this form at 2018-10.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Provided, however, that in the case of wills and codicils only the number and date of the document shall be inserted in such list
provisions.why_relevant: A second illustration of the same legislative policy: even the monthly return a notary must make to the Registrar of Lands excludes the duplicate of a will and discloses only its number and date. It confirms that the confidentiality of a will attested by a notary is not displaced by the Ordinance's own reporting duties. Supporting only.
provisions.temporal_note: Rule (26) was amended by 47-2011 s.3 (inserting sub-paragraph (a)(ii)) and by 6-2024 s.3(8) (substituting 'Form F 1' for 'Form F' in (a)(i)). Neither touches the wills proviso quoted here, which was in force at 2018-10. The excerpt deliberately stops short of the Form reference for that reason.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
provisions.why_relevant: Shows that rule (1) is penal and not merely hortatory: a notary who divulges is guilty of an offence triable summarily, on top of any civil liability. Supporting; the answer to 'should he divulge' does not depend on the size of the penalty.
provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text of s.34 is the section substituted by 31-2022 s.17, which post-dates the matter. A penalty for breach of the section 31 rules existed at 2018-10 (the earlier s.34, with fines as increased by the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005), but the pre-2022 wording and the exact fine are not in the corpus, so the excerpt must not be treated as the text in force in October 2018 and this provision is not indispensable.
provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and the cross-reference to rule (1) is real, but the corpus text of s.34 is the section wholly repealed and substituted by 31-2022 s.17, so it cannot be quoted as the penalty provision in force at 2018-10; it stays supporting only, and the gold answer's citation of s.34(1)(a) as the applicable penalty at the matter date is anachronistic.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The Notaries Ordinance imposes the duty of secrecy in terms that are complete on their face: a prohibition, plus two exhaustive exceptions (express permission of the employer, or legal compulsion). Applying them to the facts - a living testator who has given no permission, children who are not the notary's employer, and no legal process requiring disclosure - yields the whole answer. No judicial gloss or Roman-Dutch doctrine is needed to say that the notary must not answer the children's inquiry. Case law would matter only for questions this one does not ask, such as the notary's position once the testator dies or once a court compels production.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the fact that a named person executed a will before the notary, together with its date and number, is a secret confided to the notary or of which he became possessed in the execution of his office.

Whether either statutory exception to the duty of secrecy is available - express permission of the notary's employer, or a legal requirement to disclose - where the testator is alive, has not authorised disclosure, and the request comes from his children without any court order or statutory demand.
Whether the children's relationship to the testator, as persons who may later take under the will, gives them any entitlement to the information during the testator's lifetime.

questions.hop_count_basis: One directly applicable provision. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) states the prohibition and its two exceptions in the same sentence, so no definition, exception or linked section outside it has to be reached to answer. Rules (24) and (26) and s.34 corroborate but removing them would leave every required claim still supported, so they are not counted.

enrichment.original_background: The children of a testator inquire from the Notary as to whether he has attested a Will executed by their father. The testator is alive.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. D. A. Sirisena, a notary public practising in the Gampaha district, attested a last will bearing No. 1247 of his protocol, executed by Mr. Piyadasa Wickramaratne of Kadawatha on 12 March 2016, and retains the protocol of that will in his office. On 3 October 2018 the testator's two adult children, Nimal Wickramaratne and Kanthi Wickramaratne, call at the notary's office and ask him whether their father has executed a will before him and, if so, what it contains. Their father is alive and living at Kadawatha. He has given the notary no permission, oral or written, to speak about the matter to anyone, and the children produce no authority from him. They produce no order of court and no notice or demand from any officer requiring the notary to disclose the document or its particulars; they say only that they expect to inherit and wish to know where they stand.

added_facts.fact: The notary is Mr. D. A. Sirisena, a notary public practising in the Gampaha district; the testator is Mr. Piyadasa Wickramaratne of Kadawatha; the inquiring children are his two adult children, Nimal Wickramaratne and Kanthi Wickramaratne.
added_facts.reason: The original background names no party, which the classification flagged as a missing party_identity. Naming the notary, the testator and the inquirers makes the scenario determinate without changing the legal position of anyone.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None. Substituting other names or another district leaves the analysis identical.

added_facts.fact: The instrument concerned is a last will bearing No. 1247 of the notary's protocol, executed before him on 12 March 2016, and the notary retains the protocol of it in his office.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the missing relevant_document and instrument_date, and fixes the fact that the notary's knowledge arose in the execution of his office rather than socially.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: A different number or date would not change the outcome. If instead the notary had never attested any will for this testator, the question would not arise; but he would still be barred from discussing what instructions, if any, he had received.

added_facts.fact: The testator is alive, has given the notary no permission of any kind to disclose the matter, and the children produce no authority from him.
added_facts.reason: Closes the first statutory exception. The original text says only that the testator is alive; it leaves open whether he had authorised disclosure.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the testator had given the notary express permission to tell his children, the exception in rule (1) would apply and the notary could disclose to the extent permitted.

added_facts.fact: The children produce no order of court and no notice or demand from any officer requiring the notary to disclose the will or its particulars; they rely only on their expectation of inheriting.
added_facts.reason: Closes the second statutory exception, so that the prohibition in rule (1) operates without qualification.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a court had ordered production, or an officer entitled to inspect the notary's records had called for them under the Ordinance, the notary would be required to do so by law and the exception would apply.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary may tell the adult children of a living testator that he has attested a will executed by their father, and disclose its particulars, when the testator has given no permission and no legal process compels disclosure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) makes it the duty of every notary not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The two exceptions are exhaustive: consent must come from the person who employed him, and the alternative is a legal requirement to disclose, not a moral or family claim. The Ordinance treats a will as peculiarly confidential even in the notary's own compliance duties. Under s.31 rule (24) he must preserve the will as his protocol and keep a register of his instruments, but for wills and codicils only the number and date go into the register; and under the proviso to s.31 rule (26)(a)(i) the duplicate of a will is not sent to the Registrar of Lands, only its number and date appearing in the monthly list. Breach of rule (1) is an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, under s.34(1)(a).
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that Mr. Wickramaratne had executed a will, and learned what it says, because the will was executed before him and he holds the protocol; that is knowledge of which he became possessed in the execution of his office and it falls squarely within s.31 rule (1). His employer for this purpose is the testator, the person at whose instance he attested the instrument, and the testator is alive and has given no permission, express or otherwise, for the matter to be disclosed. The children are not his employer; their expectation of inheriting gives them no present interest in the document, because nothing passes under a will until the testator's death, and no authority from their father is produced. Nor is the second exception engaged: no court has ordered production and no officer entitled under the Ordinance to inspect his records has called for them, so he is not required to do so by law. Confirming even the bare fact that a will exists would divulge the substance of what the testator confided, and the Ordinance's own treatment of wills, which keeps their particulars out of both the notary's register and his return to the Registrar of Lands, tells against any narrower reading. Should the notary answer, he would expose himself to prosecution and civil liability under s.34.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. He should decline, politely and without hinting at the answer either way, and tell the children that he is not at liberty to say whether he has attested any instrument for their father and that they must ask their father himself; if the testator authorises disclosure, or if the notary is later required by law to disclose, the position changes, and it changes again on the testator's death, when the will falls to be dealt with in the ordinary way.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
That duty yields only in two cases: where the notary has the express permission of his employer, or where he is required by law to disclose.
A will executed before a notary is preserved by him as his protocol, and only the number and date of a will are entered in the register he is obliged to keep.
In the monthly return a notary makes to the Registrar of Lands, wills and codicils are identified by number and date alone.
A notary who acts in breach of the duty of secrecy commits an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
The notary's knowledge that the testator executed a will, and of its contents, was acquired in the execution of his office, because the will was executed before him and he holds its protocol.
The testator, and not his children, is the notary's employer for the purposes of the permission exception, and the testator is alive and has given no permission.
The second exception is not engaged either, because no court order and no lawful demand requiring disclosure has been made on the notary.
Confirming that a will exists would itself divulge what the testator confided, and the statutory practice of recording wills by number and date alone tells against a narrower reading of the duty.
The notary should not divulge the information and should decline the children's inquiry, referring them to their father.
If the notary were to answer the inquiry he would expose himself to prosecution and to civil liability.
The position would change if the testator gave express permission, or if the notary were later required by law to disclose.

questions.block_reason: Core answer verified: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) is verbatim, is untouched by 20-1976 s.10, 47-2011 ss.2-3, 31-2022 s.16 and 6-2024 s.3, and was in force at 2018-10, and the conclusion that the notary must not divulge follows from it. Two things need a lawyer before this stands as gold. First, the gold answer's rule and conclusion paragraphs state the penalty for breach of rule (1) by reference to s.34(1)(a), but the only s.34 in the corpus is the section repealed and substituted by 31-2022 s.17; the pre-2022 penalty section is not held, so claims CL-M103-Q01-005 and CL-M103-Q01-011 cannot be verified at the matter date and are marked disputed. Second, the answer identifies the testator as the notary's employer for the permission exception and asserts that the children have no present interest because nothing passes under a will until death; neither proposition has an anchor in the corpus, since employer is undefined in the Ordinance (s.43 defines only three terms) and the Wills Ordinance No. 21 of 1844 as held here says nothing about the ambulatory character of a will, so CL-M103-Q01-007 and ISS-M103-Q01-03 are marked disputed. Dropping the two s.34 sentences from the prose and settling the employer reading would restore proposed_gold; the authority requirement remains statute_only either way.
